extraction.name: CADS: A Comprehensive Anatomical Dataset and Segmentation for Whole-Body Anatomy in Computed Tomography
extraction.description: A large-scale whole-body CT dataset and segmentation framework comprising 22,022 CT volumes with annotations for 167 anatomical structures, created through systematic integration, standardization, pseudo-labeling, quality control, and refinement of heterogeneous multi-source data, with accompanying open-source models and a 3D Slicer plugin.

extraction.citeAs: Xu, M., Amiranashvili, T., Navarro, F., et al. CADS: A Comprehensive Anatomical Dataset and Segmentation for Whole-Body Anatomy in Computed Tomography. arXiv:2507.22953v1, 2025.
extraction.rai:dataCollection: The dataset aggregates 22,022 CT volumes from 40 diverse sources, including large-scale public archives, medical imaging challenges, focused research studies, hospital cohorts, 484 newly acquired anonymized head CTs, and 586 newly released triphasic contrast-enhanced abdominal CT scans. The collection spans over 100 imaging facilities across 16 countries and includes healthy subjects and various pathological conditions. The authors systematically consolidated CT scans and annotations from public repositories and newly contributed data, then generated annotations for all 167 structures using a multi-stage pseudo-labeling pipeline with specialized models, shape-informed quality control, ensemble-based label selection, and final model training.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Secondary Data analysis, Experiments, Manual Human Curator, Direct measurement
extraction.rai:dataCollectionMissingData: Approximately 79% of the initial collection did not include any manual annotations, and only 4,695 of 22,022 scans (21%) contained partial annotations from public sources.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Raw data consist of volumetric CT scans collected from 40 sources, including TotalSegmentator, NLST, CT-RATE, AbdomenCT-1K, Grand Challenge and MICCAI challenge datasets, TCIA studies, SAROS, VISCERAL, and newly acquired anonymized head CT scans from Istanbul Medipol University and triphasic contrast-enhanced abdominal CT scans from TUM Klinikum Rechts der Isar.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: The authors generated full annotations through whole-body pseudo-labeling using nine specialized models, filtered unreliable pseudo-labels using shape-informed quality control based on neural implicit functions, trained three complementary model flavors (GT-flavor, Pseudo-flavor, Shape-flavor), statistically selected the best-performing flavor per structure, assembled final labels with original ground-truth annotations taking priority, and applied post-processing refinements for head-region hallucinations and rib segmentation correction including costovertebral joint retrieval.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: All images were reoriented to the standard RAS convention, resampled to a uniform 1.5 mm isotropic resolution, and affine matrices were simplified by removing rotation and translation components while preserving scaling and shear. For newly acquired hospital head CT scans, a Gaussian filter (sigma = 5 voxels at 1.5 mm spacing) was applied to facial regions for privacy protection. Additional preprocessing included interpolation of sparse SAROS slice annotations into dense 3D labels and targeted cropping/filtering for head-region pseudo-labels.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Annotations came from original manual, hybrid, and algorithmic labels in source datasets, plus new manual annotations by three in-house medical research assistants and a radiation oncologist on the VISCERAL Gold Corpus for critical radiotherapy structures. For the full CADS-dataset, annotations for all 167 structures were generated using pseudo-labeling with specialized nnU-Net models across nine anatomical groups, followed by shape-based quality control, multi-strategy label optimization across GT, pseudo, and shape flavors, and replacement with original ground-truth labels when available. A significant portion of the unseen TotalSegmentator test set was manually reviewed by in-house medical professionals to classify annotations as reliable or unreliable.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: The authors analyzed annotation quality through shape-informed likelihood estimation in shape space using neural implicit functions and 90-percentile Hausdorff distance to rank pseudo-label quality. They statistically compared three model flavors per structure using Dice and HD95 with Shapiro-Wilk, Levene, ANOVA, Welch’s ANOVA, Kruskal-Wallis, Tukey’s HSD, and Dunn’s tests to select the best label source. They also manually reviewed TotalSegmentator test annotations, documenting recurrent errors such as mislabeling between adjacent structures, missing segments, over-segmentation, and boundary inaccuracies, and excluded unreliable structures from final evaluation.
extraction.rai:annotatorDemographics: Three in-house medical research assistants, a radiation oncologist (JCP), in-house medical professionals for test set review, and an experienced radiation oncologist with 5.5 years in practice for clinical expert review.
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: nnU-Net; neural implicit functions; vesselFM; ANTS non-rigid transformation
extraction.rai:personalSensitiveInformation: Facial features in newly acquired hospital head CT scans; patient age (patients aged ≥18 years); geography/country of acquisition; pathology and disease status; imaging facility/institution source. Facial regions were anonymized by Gaussian blurring for privacy.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: The paper states that by making the dataset, models, and clinical software tool publicly available, the authors aim to advance robust AI solutions in radiology and make comprehensive anatomical analysis accessible to clinicians and researchers. They describe clinical potential in radiation oncology, diagnostic radiology, and large-scale population studies, and position CADS as a bridge between technical capabilities and clinical applications supporting AI-integrated healthcare workflows.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The paper discusses systematic bias errors in existing datasets, particularly in complex structures like ribs and vertebrae, which can be learned and propagated by models. It also notes that their automated annotation approach aims to reduce variance-driven errors through multi-source data integration, large-scale training, ensemble selection, and shape-based outlier detection, while targeted anatomical refinements address systematic omissions such as costovertebral joints.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The authors identify several limitations: shape-based quality assessment excludes low-quality segmentations rather than correcting them, potentially removing pathological cases with atypical anatomy and limiting learning of edge scenarios; coverage currently spans head to knees and excludes hands and feet; some structures require refinement, including brain mask definition, optic chiasm under-segmentation, omitted superior heart portions, short rectum extent, trachea limited to air content, and imprecise vena cava delineation; facial features are intentionally anonymized, limiting detailed facial analysis; and the modular specialized-model design could be replaced by future unified architectures.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is intended to enable development of whole-body CT segmentation models and support further research in medical imaging. The paper describes use cases including training segmentation models, anatomical landmark detection, cross-modality registration, anatomy-guided synthesis, longitudinal organ tracking, personalized anatomical modeling, radiation treatment planning, diagnostic radiology applications, and large-scale population studies. The CADS-model is also provided as a 3D Slicer plugin for clinical and research use.
